outlet: U.S. Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
title: As EPA Rolls Back Power Plant Emissions Rules, Whitehouse & Casten Introduce New Legislation to Restore Agency’s Core Mission
description:
Environmental Health Restoration Act would reinstate pre-Trump environmental safeguards and hold polluters accountable
Washington, D.C. – Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, and Representative Sean Casten (D-IL) last week introduced the Environmental Health Restoration Act, legislation to restore and strengthen the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) core mission to protect public health and the environment. 

The bill comes just days after the Trump EPA finalized the repeal of the 2024 greenhouse gas standards for coal- and gas-fired power plants and moved to eliminate remaining federal climate pollution requirements for the power sector to bail out Trump’s fossil fuel donors.

“The Trump EPA has fully abandoned its decades-long duty to protect Americans’ health and safety.  Its relentless attacks on science have delivered for big political donors while poisoning our air and water and speeding up the climate crisis,” said Whitehouse.  “Our bill would jumpstart the process of restoring the science, the scientists, and the original mission guiding the EPA.”

“At a time when the Trump Administration is ignoring the climate crisis and undermining Americans’ ability to breathe clean air, drink clean water, and enjoy the outdoors, it is more important than ever to restore a commitment to science-based environmental protection at the EPA,” said Casten.  “The EPA was created to protect public health and our environment.  I’m proud to introduce this legislation to refocus the agency on its core mission.”

On Wednesday, Whitehouse and Casten joined Protect Our Winters, former EPA scientist Stuart Nissenbaum, League of Conservation Voters, and Olympic athletes for a press conference to speak about their experiences of a worsening climate and the need to reinstate these protections.

“As an Olympian training in the mountains all over the world, I’ve seen less and less snow, glaciers shrinking at a not-so-glacial pace, and volatile air quality,” said Tommy Ford, three-time Olympian and World Cup Champion.  “This directly affects our community’s health and economy.  A stronger, more durable EPA is essential for clean air, clean water and a strong, healthy community.”

“Rolling back environmental protections has real consequences for the places and experiences that define the outdoor community,” said Ben Gubits, Vice President of Campaigns at Protect Our Winters.  “It means dirtier air, greater climate pollution, more threats to public health and accelerating damage to our winters, waterways and public lands.  The Environmental Health Restoration Act draws a clear line, the EPA must follow science, enforce the law and put people ahead of polluters.  This is a positive vision for the future looking well beyond the Trump years.”

The Environmental Health Restoration Act responds to recent deregulatory actions that have weakened or delayed protections governing air pollution, water quality, greenhouse gas emissions, and environmental enforcement.  It would reaffirm Congress’s intent that the EPA follow independent science and the law, regulate harmful pollution and the polluters who cause it, and protect communities from harm.  Specifically, the Environmental Health Restoration Act would:


Restore key protections for pollution from power plants, vehicles, and oil and gas operations that were in effect on January 19, 2025.
Require EPA decisions to be grounded in peer-reviewed science and restore independent scientific advisory bodies.
Rebuild the agency’s civil and criminal enforcement capacity and require annual accountability reporting to Congress.
Prioritize monitoring and enforcement in communities facing disproportionate pollution burdens.
Require public-health and cumulative-impact analyses for EPA actions affecting air and water quality.
Preserve states’ ability to adopt environmental standards stronger than federal requirements.
Allow people harmed by the EPA’s failure to comply with the law to seek relief in federal court.

Senators Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Ron Wyden (D-OR) cosponsor the legislation in the Senate.  The bill is endorsed by Protect Our Winters, League of Conservation Voters, and the Natural Resources Defense Council.

Text of the legislation can be found here.

title: A recent Fifth Circuit decision could have significant implications for how the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) evaluates and manages chemical risks under the Toxic Substances Control Act… | Arnold & Porter
description:
A recent Fifth Circuit decision could have significant implications for how the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) evaluates and manages chemical risks under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA).

In East Fork Enterprises, Inc. v. EPA, the court vacated EPA’s risk management rule for methylene chloride, as well as the underlying determination of unreasonable risk. The decision addresses several key aspects of EPA’s approach under TSCA, including the “whole chemical” approach to risk evaluations, assumptions regarding the use of personal protective equipment, the meaning of “unreasonable risk,” and the extent to which EPA must consider costs and other burdens when developing risk management measures.

The impact could extend well beyond methylene chloride, potentially affecting existing and future EPA risk evaluations and risk management rules under TSCA.

In the latest Environmental Edge blog post, Arnold & Porter attorneys Camille Heyboer, Lawrence E. Culleen, Brandon W. Neuschafer, and Katrina R. Umstead break down five key takeaways from the decision and what they could mean for EPA’s administration of TSCA.

title: Prenatal exposure to aromatic amines and associations with infant cognition in the ECHO.CA.IL cohorts - Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
description: Aromatic amines (AAs) are carcinogenic compounds widely used in consumer products. However, few studies have assessed exposure to AAs during pregnancy, and no human studies have examined associations between AAs and infant cognition, despite in vitro evidence of neurotoxicity. We conducted an analysis of prenatal AA exposure and infant cognitive outcomes using a subset of the Illinois Kids Development Study and Chemicals in Our Bodies, two prospective birth cohorts that together make up ECHO.CA.IL (N = 250). AAs, including aniline, o/m-toluidine, 4-chloroaniline, o-anisidine, 4,4’methylenedianiline, and cotinine, were measured in 2nd trimester urine samples and detected in >50% of participants. Infant cognition was assessed using a visual recognition memory (VRM) task administered using an infrared eye tracker at 7.5 months. We used linear regression to examine associations between individual natural log transformed AAs and their molar sum with VRM outcomes. We examined effect modification and interaction by child sex. A natural log unit increase in ΣAAs and the individual analyte 4,4’methylenedianiline was associated with an increase in time to reach familiarization, suggesting poorer attention (β = 7.1, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.97, 15.16; β = 3.95, 95% CI = -0.27, 8.17, respectively). Cotinine was associated with worsening novelty preference (β=-0.01, 95% CI = -0.02, 0), indicating poorer working memory. Aniline was associated with an increase in time to reach familiarization only among females (p-value for interaction=0.06).
